titel: Pasteurised, UHT, raw: what heat does to milk
kurz: Milk is heated to kill pathogens. The hotter, the longer it keeps, but the more it tastes cooked.
bild_im_kopf: Like a thermostat for shelf life: every extra degree buys time and costs a little freshness.
was_passiert: To pasteurise, milk is briefly heated to 72 to 75 °C for 15 to 30 seconds. That kills pathogens but not all bacteria, so it belongs in the fridge. UHT milk is heated above 135 °C for a few seconds and packed sterile: unopened it keeps for months. In the process, [[milchzucker|milk sugar]] and protein react a little with each other, and sulphur compounds are released from the protein. That is where the slight cooked taste comes from.
warum_wichtig: For yoghurt, fresh cheese or cheese it matters how the milk was treated: strongly heated protein curdles differently. And raw milk from the farm can contain pathogens.
faustregeln: For raw milk: bring it to the boil before drinking, because it can contain pathogens.
For fresh cheese and cheese: no UHT milk, because its strongly heated protein curdles only soft and crumbly.
Homogenised means the fat has been broken into tiny droplets, so the cream no longer rises.
schritte: Bring raw milk from a farm or milk vending machine to the boil before drinking it.
Stir constantly and keep the heat medium so nothing catches on the bottom of the pan.
Cool boiled milk quickly and keep it in the fridge.
For homemade yoghurt use pasteurised or UHT milk, not raw.
